utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, this morning we are to have a witness by videolink.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not getting any translation. Just a minute. I'm not having any translation into English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's going to be fine now. Can you hear the interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic. I do apologise. This comes from dealing with too many matters at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, before we start our work today, I have to share some information with you regarding the remaining five witnesses that should be examined by Thursday. I don't think that there will be any problems. We should be able to deal with that. But I have to say that we have had excellent cooperation with the witness and victims unit and I'm sure that we will continue having such cooperation with them in the future because we managed to solve even the problems that cropped up over the past few days with joint efforts. First, we had problems with the witness who did not have a passport and we managed to procure a passport for him on Saturday. He was supposed to be here on Friday, and there were some problems about witness T-57. The witness who obtained his passport on Saturday is T-25. Two witnesses, one of whom I wanted to examine today were supposed to be here on the 21st of June [sic], Saturday, but they arrived last night after 9.00 p.m. I intended to proof one of them and to examine him today but it was impossible to proof him yesterday because he arrived at 9.30 p.m. and it was impossible for me to do anything about proofing him because it is against the rules to proof a witness at such a late hour, in light of the fact that this witness had travelled. But we managed to resolve all those problems and I am sure that all these witnesses will be examined by Thursday. But after the first witness on our list for today, I don't have another witness available for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you appear to have been caught in a set of circumstances over which you had very little control, and in those circumstances, the Chamber has to understand your position. Of course, we want to make the best use of the Court's time. It is regrettable that you'll have no witnesses after the first witness, but I must stress that the last day for this session will be Thursday. We are not sitting on Friday. Let us proceed with the videolink for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have another request to make. I have already contacted my learned colleague Mr. Waespi, and this is not because we don't have another witness for today, but because in the opinion of the Defence this witness is very important. We first asked for one hour for each side and the Court decided to allot 30 minutes, and, Your Honours, I really am asking you it will be difficult to examine this witness in half an hour via videolink. We have to use a video-clip that lasts five minutes, tender some documents and the witness has to tell us something about himself. But I would like to ask you therefore to allot some more time for us to examine this witness via videolink. That's not because we don't have another witness lined up after this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how much time would that be? 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that 30 more minutes -- in fact what we asked for originally, one hour, that that should be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Ms. Edgerton, you're rising to support the application for the extended time?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can deal with this witness in whatever time is allotted but for everyone's information once the witness is sworn in, I will be raising objections on the use of the video and some of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll grant you one hour, Mr. Tapuskovic. Now, let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We have to use our time as efficiently as possible and speed things up as much as we can. I first have to do what I have to do to introduce you to the Trial Chamber. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges your full name?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Milosav Gagovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born on the 12th of August 1938?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Am I going too fast?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You're doing fine. In the village of Pluzine in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your elementary education in Niksic in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went on to start the secondary education in Niksic too?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you graduated from the secondary military school in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You graduated from the military academy, the studies lasted for four years, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are also a graduate of the command and staff school in Belgrade; that course of studies took two years to complete?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are a retired colonel of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From 1968, you lived and worked in Sarajevo in the military school centre, teaching the course in the department for firearms?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you were the assistant Commander of the 4th Corps for logistics?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Commander of the 4th Corps, your commander, was Major General Djurdjevac?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague from the Prosecution will now object to the testimony of this witness. That's what she indicated, that she would be objecting to the testimony of this witness. Well, probably when the time comes. So, Mr. Gagovic, let us continue. Could you tell us briefly something about your job in the Yugoslav People's Army at the time when the conflict broke out? So could you please tell us first what barracks were you? Where was your workplace?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I was at the corps command, as you indicated I was the assistant commander for logistics, and I did my work in this sphere. I was a member of the collegium of the corps commander, and because of that, I was acquainted with all the work and all the activities that the 4th Corps command was engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of May, I was appointed the representative of the 4th Corps commander after General Djurdjevac retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you, thank you. That will be enough for now. I will now continue with my questions. Mr. Gagovic, you've just explained to us what you were. How many barracks were there in Sarajevo, in the area of responsibility of the 4th Corps where you did your work, as you just explained to us?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The barracks in Sarajevo were located at Lukavica, that was under the command of the 4th Corps and the other barracks, Marsal Tito, Jusuf Dzonlic, the Jajce barracks, Viktor Bubanj, Pazaric barracks. Those were the barracks where units belonging to other formations were stationed. But in the disciplinary sense, they were all subordinate to the 4th Corps command because it was the most senior command in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My next question to you is as follows: Sarajevo was the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It had those barracks, and I assume that there were troops in those barracks. In the 40 years from the Second World War until that time, was the situation there identical to any other city in the former country?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Definitely. It was completely the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I find that to be a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if it could be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is leading. It has to be reformulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, could you please tell me, you were there from 1968.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the time of your arrival there, that's 1968, until this time, were troops stationed in those areas at all times?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The military was stationed in Sarajevo, and it was held in high esteem and it contributed greatly to the preparations of Sarajevo for the 14th winter Olympics. And many officers were -- received commendations, awards, from the city council, and everybody was held in high esteem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was that the case throughout the country when it came to the army?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Since I served in Slovenia and in Croatia, I went to school in Serbia and in Montenegro where I was born, I also served in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I can say that I covered the entire country and I can tell you that everywhere in the country, the army was held in great respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us move on to 1991, which is why you are asked to come here and testify. In the course of 1991, and in early 1992, through the chain of command, through your position, did you learn anything about the events in Slovenia and Croatia and other parts of the country, including Bosnia and Herzegovina, but not concerning Sarajevo? Were you able to learn what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Through the chain of command--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Please stop. Don't answer the question. Ms. Edgerton, is it relevance or -- what is your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What's the relevance of this, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was expecting this question and I have prepared very well to reply. First of all, let me refer you to paragraph 7 of the indictment, but even beyond that, I would have called many more witnesses had I disputed the agreed facts. Agreed fact number 5, in June of 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared independence from SFRY and under the circumstances that ensued, they tried to gain recognition as sovereign states. That had an impact on Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. This is paragraph 5 of the agreed facts, and this can be found in the judgement in paragraph 194. Item 9 of the agreed facts, and this be found in paragraph 195 of the judgement, it reads as follows: "Until the end in 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army further in the text JNA withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia and headed towards strategic positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina." And finally, in order to clarify this even more, item 17 of agreed facts, paragraph 196, where it says, "In April of 1992, based on the decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the loyal units of Territorial Defence, together with paramilitary groups of Bosnian Croats, paramilitary forces, and Muslim forces were all incorporated into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, hereinafter the army of BH." So this is the relevancy. This is why this witness is so relevant. I have to refer you back to these agreed or established facts which are very important in order to understand the events that ensued in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, I can continue to refer to you to paragraphs that are all listed in our briefs, when we asked that this witness be called here to testify. There are further ten paragraphs that confirm this, and this all is linked to paragraph 7, to the established facts which are very important and can all be linked to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, isn't the point of agreed facts that the parties don't have to lead evidence on it because it's agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I have a right to challenge them. I'm entitled to that. That is one of my basic rights. I have to challenge some of those facts, and I have to tender through this witness some documents that illustrate these facts when it comes to Slovenia and Croatia. So far, these documents have not been used here, since this has to do with paragraph 5 and especially paragraph 9, which was not fully recognised in the Galic judgement at all. Because the documents that I have to introduce through this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are saying you have to challenge these facts that -- to which you have agreed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to understand the context, it says here, it had an impact on Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then the rest of the text follows. I do not intend to challenge everything, but in order for you to understand what this is about, I have to tender several documents which are even more illustrative when it comes to the entire problem. It's not just this. A lot of other facts emerge based on these documents which completes the picture and challenges some other facts. It reinforces some facts and brings into question some other facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I can see that even if the facts are agreed, you may still wish to use them. The point of agreeing it, though, is that there should be no dispute between the parties about the existence of those facts during the Court proceedings. Ms. Edgerton, he says that he's adducing this evidence as part of the context, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He may say he's adducing this evidence as part of the context but the argument he's painted, Your Honour, with respect, is one of rebuttal of adjudicated facts. And if my friend is rebutting, for example, with respect to adjudicated fact number 5, which says in June of 1991, Slovenia and Croatia declared independence from the SFRY and tried to gain recognition from sovereign states, I gather that by this line of questioning, he's disputing the fact that Slovenia and Croatia declared independence from the SFRY. So perhaps he could actually clarify his position in rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you talking about agreed facts or adjudicated facts? Because there is a difference. Of course, you have a right to rebut adjudicated facts. Which is it, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm dealing now with adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I listed some of them. Item 5 of the adjudicated facts, especially towards the end, where it says that everything that took place in Slovenia had an impact on Bosnia and Herzegovina. These documents, and I can tell you which documents I'm talking about, there are three of them, and they deal with the work of the Presidency of the SFRY at the time which was headed by Stipe Mesic. Based on these documents, you can see that certain things were announced and then took place, and that they happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the same way they happened in Slovenia and Croatia. These documents speak of those events, and they are not referred to in the judgement. However, these documents explain the broader context in a legal sense and then there is also the issue of the transformation of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Adjudicated fact number 5 reads, Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence from the SFRY in June 1991. During the following months, they strove to establish themselves as sovereign states. This had an impact in BiH. So what aspect of that are you seeking to rebut by this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to rebut much that follows after that. I haven't got time to read all of that. There is a number of facts listed here. As I told you, I could refer you to many of them. But what it says here, in a short sentence, this had an impact on Bosnia and Herzegovina as well. There is a whole number of wrong aspects here, and this will be illustrated by the documents that I intend to show to the witness because this witness knows quite a lot about them. There is a number of facts that were established here, adjudicated. We did not agree to all of them, and we do acknowledge that it had an impact on Bosnia and Herzegovina but not the impact described in this judgement and I can tell you exactly which facts we challenge. The documents that I intend to introduce through this witness rebut a number of other established or adjudicated facts which you intend to use in the proceedings against Dragomir Milosevic. I could list at least 20 to 30 such items but I don't think it's necessary if I explain to you the context that this witness is about to give evidence and to indicate some other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll proceed this way, Mr. Tapuskovic. We'll hear you putting the evidence to the witness which you say rebuts item 5 in the adjudicated facts, and we'll make a determination as we go along on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order to make it as clear as possible, when we continue I would kindly ask you to look at item 9 of adjudicated facts where it says, "Until the end of 1991, the JNA withdrew from Slovenia and Croatia and headed towards strategic positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina." This is perhaps one of the key items that Defence has to contest because the army had been in place there since 1945 until the conflict erupted, and it could never withdraw towards any strategic positions. This is the decisive issue for all of us here and through the evidence of this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us hear the evidence, and we'll decide it on an individual basis. We'll decide the question of admissibility on an individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But as you proceed with this type of evidence, then you must direct us to the adjudicated fact that it seeks to rebut. For example, you just mentioned adjudicated fact number 9. So that's the way I'd like you to proceed, just tell us the adjudicated fact to which the evidence relates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm now referring to 5, 9 and 17. First of all, primarily item 9. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, where had you come from and how many troops were there in 1968 or in the year that we are dealing with, 1992? Had you arrived there from somewhere else or were you there already in 1968, and if so, with whom?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I came to Sarajevo in 1968 in order to attend the school for infantry officers, and I came there with other officers from Rijeka. I received an order to -- moving me there, to the centre of military schools, and I remained in Sarajevo until 1992. I remained there continuously, except for the time when I went to Belgrade to attend the military academy, following which I returned back to Sarajevo to serve in the command of the 7th military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you command? Were there any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I worked with cadets of the secondary military school. There were soldiers there who served the army, and I also later worked at the barracks in Lukavica, naturally every army has soldiers and commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On average, how many troops were there in such a school centre throughout all those years and decades?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not rising with an objection but I actually find because they speak the same language, Mr. Tapuskovic is speaking again before the interpretation is -- into English is finished and it poses some difficulty for me. I don't know about the rest of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, that's true. Please ensure that you don't overlap, Mr. Tapuskovic and witness. Please ensure that you observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, how many soldiers, rank and file soldiers, were there in such centres, in centres such as Sarajevo doing their national service?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the average, two or three thousand. That would depend on each generation of recruits. And there were also cadets from the military high school and from the military academy, the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the case in all the other centres in Slovenia, in Croatia, in Macedonia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in all the other republics of what was then the former state?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly, that was the case. It was the same in Rijeka, in Slovenia, in Crnomelj where I was, in Sarajevo. It would all depend on the actual specialisation of the unit, its place in the establishment and so on, but otherwise it was all the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell the Judges about your knowledge of the events in 1991 and 1992 in Slovenia, Croatia and some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the break-up of the single-party system in 1990, the army was depoliticized. Politics was no longer involved in the JNA. It was in the barracks and it dealt with its own business. In 1991, we learned that one part of the Slovenian nation in Slovenia and the same thing went for Croatia and later on in Bosnia, does not have a proper attitude towards the members of the Yugoslav People's Army. And once Slovenia declared its independence as an independent republic, the most reckless move was made, the barracks were blockaded, our power lines, water supply lines, were cut, and it went as far as the maltreatment of the families of the JNA officers. We received those reports regularly from the 1st military district command and from the political administration, and we also were in direct contact with our colleagues serving in Slovenia, and we -- and Croatia. And we had Slovenians and Croats and Muslims, Serbs, all ethnic communities were represented in the corps command at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can I just see if I understand that we are not talking about Sarajevo in this regard at all. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, what are we speaking about here? Is this for Sarajevo or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not the situation in Sarajevo yet. These developments happened in Sarajevo in 1992 but this was the situation as it evolved first in Slovenia, then it spilled over to Croatia. And only in 1992 did we encounter this kind of situation in Sarajevo or in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague from the Prosecution got to her feet to object and she was right in doing so, but now you were telling us about those most terrible things, you came to a point where some really terrible things started to happen to the soldiers in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the most difficult thing for us was when we learned that some units in Slovenia came under armed attack. First, the border units then the units in smaller garrisons and those larger units in larger garrisons and barracks were blockaded and some moves were made that nobody could really allow. The power lines and the water supply lines were cut and this forced the JNA's hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're talking about power and water. You don't say anything about any casualties?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were casualties. I don't know the exact figure but it was more than 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please stop. Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've just gone through the adjudicated facts and there is, with respect, no mention of any evidence that might relate to blockades or attacks on barracks in Slovenia, which is the area we have been dealt with and sometime I submit that this doesn't go to the adjudicated facts in any regard and is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, to make things perfectly clear for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'm calling on you to respond to the objection and then I will make my ruling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the end, the witness said that soldiers were killed and that to his knowledge 46 soldiers were killed in Slovenia to his knowledge. I wanted to find out what was happening in Sarajevo in the beginning of 1992. Was it the same thing? I have to take it step by step in my work. I couldn't simply ask him, well, could you please tell me how many soldiers were killed in Sarajevo if any and what is the relationship, what is the link between what happened in Slovenia and what happened in Sarajevo? This is what I have to ask him next. My next question in relation to what was happening in Slovenia, what had been announced in advance and about what was happening in Sarajevo. I want to ask him whether he knew anything about it. Was it the same thing that had happened in Slovenia that was now happening in Sarajevo, in the streets of Sarajevo? I can't ask those questions without going step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Bring the witness now to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, could you please, then, tell us after all those events that you just told us about, what happened in Sarajevo in March, February, and in particular April 1992, and that had to do with the army, first of all?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the same scenario that unfolded in Slovenia and Croatia started to unfold in Sarajevo and Bosnia and Herzegovina. First of all, let me say that the JNA had an agreement with the BH government to set up a joint, mixed police and military units that would control all the vehicles --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, sir, Mr. Gagovic, I have to ask you to give us the most drastic events in March and in April because the political aspect of it we have in writing. What did you, as a commander, and your troops go through in March and April, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to establish a link between this agreement that was complied with until the 2nd of May 1992. And as for the -- what was happening with the paramilitaries in Sarajevo and in Bosnia and Herzegovina in March, there were no such activities. The only exception is that the HVO forces from Croatia moved in the Slavonski Brod area into Bosnia-Herzegovina and the same thing happened in Neum where they moved towards Prozor and some paramilitaries joined them. This is what happened in Gorazde Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, we have very little time. Could you please tell me what happened in the streets of Sarajevo in March and April? Could you just give me a direct answer to this question?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in March and April, there were no conflicts between the paramilitary forces of the BH and JNA in March and April. There were conflicts with the forces that had arrived from Croatia into the Bosnian territory. But in the town itself, some paramilitaries killed some ethnic Serbs, among them was the Nikola Gardovic a guest at the Serbian wedding, an athlete, a police officer, Pero Perovic, the Trifunovic brothers and so on. And in May, the conflicts broke out that you were asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened in May?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 2nd of May, I said that we had this agreement with the Minister of the Interior that all the units, movements were to be announced and logistics units that were supplying the military district command headed out towards Bistrica from the Viktor Bubanj barracks to the army district command. And in Skenderija, it was ambushed by the paramilitaries or at that time those were perhaps not paramilitaries any more than military units. It was -- it came under attack and the JNA centre came under attack. The military factory and the barracks were blockaded and an attack was launched on the Butmir airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to show you a video clip with the approval of the Trial Chamber. It lasts 55 minutes but the Defence made an excerpt lasting five minutes and then if we could watch this and then I will be asking you some questions?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, your promised objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. This is a video that the Prosecution received after 5.30 on Friday afternoon, a total of 55 minutes, not one word of it transcribed into English. We received sometime later on that evening timer numbers that the Defence counsel intended to play for the witness. So having, with some difficulty, I admit, because most machines here were unable over the weekend to play that video clip, having watched those timer numbers I would object to this being used on two grounds. First of all, the absolute late notice of this material which was not on the Defence Exhibit list in any regard and not sought to be added at any time prior to that, and the absolute irrelevance to the potential criminal liability of the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can you give us an example as to why you say it's irrelevant? Or do we have to look at one ourselves?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We could do both, Your Honour. In the Prosecution's submission this relates to the killing, death of a number of JNA soldiers in May -- either May 2nd or 3rd of 1992 in Sarajevo. But without having any access to any translation material, I'm only guessing that on the basis of the pictures that I was able to see in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that the evidence appears to relate to the killing of JNA soldiers in May 1992. Mr. Tapuskovic -- in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, we don't deny that that happened. In fact that's one of the adjudicated facts. If I have a moment I can even direct you to the related facts. Those would be number 29, 30, 31 and 32, and the Prosecution does not deny in any regard that there were some JNA soldiers killed in the context of the fighting taking place on those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, let us focus now on the two grounds on which the objection is based. First, lateness and lack of translation, and secondly, relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we disclosed this to the Prosecution as early as on Friday. This is probably the only case that something was disclosed to the other parties three days before it is exhibited in the courtroom. We had discussions with the Prosecution in -- on Friday and I think on Saturday we discussed it. The first objection was that the clip lasted 55 minutes and then we said that we would be playing only five minutes 50 seconds out of the 53 minutes. That's one thing. And we also said that we would be supplying a transcript. We've already submitted the transcript to the translation service. It contains two and a half pages of what actually contains direct order, a document. There is a very brief reply at the beginning to what the commentator is saying, and all the other things are the authentic orders issued by those people to burn, to scorch, to destroy everything before UNPROFOR arrives at the scene. So these are authentic documents that pertain to the events of the 2nd of May, and there may be some things that relate to other things happening in those days. But this is authentic material that was obtained from audiotapes. These are orders issued by certain people saying that everything should be destroyed, burned, killed, before the United Nations come. So this is a document that deserves your attention, and all you have to do is look at paragraph 29. I don't even have to mention any other items. When it says that on the 2nd of May while President Izetbegovic was in Lisbon attending negotiations, that a large attack was carried out on the town and I will now be able to show to you who carried out this attack on the basis of authentic documents. And I can also quote paragraphs 27, 44, and I don't want to now read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have here 29, item 29 of the adjudicated facts. It says on the 2nd of May 1992, a major JNA attack on the centre of Sarajevo occurred while President Izetbegovic was in Lisbon for negotiations. Now you're seeking to rebut this by saying what? You're not seeking to rebut it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not rebutting this. I'm rebutting the end of that sentence, a massive attack on the centre of Sarajevo was carried out. It was carried out by paramilitaries, and you can see it in the clip. It is suggested here that the JNA carried out this attack, where it's not the case. I intend to show that the paramilitaries attacked, not the army, and you can see the soldiers killed, and you can see how Sarajevo was torched and destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, isn't that a rebuttal? You're seeking to rebut it by showing that the attack was not carried out by the JNA but by the paramilitaries. That's my understanding of what you are doing. You're saying, yes, there was an attack but it was not done by the JNA, it was done by paramilitaries. And this clip will substantiate that, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll hear it and as for the translation, it doesn't appear to be very long so we'll listen to the interpretation. Do you have the transcripts? Do you have any translations at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, DD004360, this is in Serbian and the interpreters can interpret that. We took the transcript down. It's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Now, just advise me on this technical matter. How will the interpreters get that to translate it? Putting it on the ELMO or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We were given transcript in B/C/S, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the interpreters already have that. All right. So the interpreters have the B/C/S transcript and they will interpret that. Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the Prosecution's part hearing the argument of Mr. Tapuskovic and learning more than I certainly knew even having watched those portions of the video, I again would reinforce my objection as to the relevance and, of course, the problems and the fairness or unfairness that hearing this video at this time at such late notice would pose to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As for the first, I believe Mr. Tapuskovic has established a basis for using this video. He's using it, as I understand it, to rebut adjudicated fact number 29, which says that a major JNA attack on the centre of Sarajevo occurred. And he says this video will establish that while there was an attack, it was not done by the JNA, it was done by the paramilitaries, and I have to allow him to do that, if that's what the video will show. If the video doesn't show that, then we'll exclude it. As for the lateness, I will ensure that you're not in any way prejudiced, Ms. Edgerton, and I will address that when the time comes. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is DD00 -- well, this is the film, the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] In Bosnia and Herzegovina, since 1991 onwards, it was exposed to a continuous pressure and attacks by paramilitary formations. These paramilitary formations regardless of to what extent they pretend to be self-organised, were nevertheless, organised by the highest levels of the official BH authorities; that is to say, the Party of Democratic Action, as the representative of the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Sarajevo, daily Oslobodjenje on the 14th of September 1992, the assistant Minister of Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mole Bisic [phoen] stated that back in May 1991, Patriotic League was established as an illegal organisation which encompassed all paramilitary formations. In the daily Nacional on the 25th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop, please stop. Mr. Tapuskovic, you need to lay some kind of foundation. Who is speaking? And when was the video made? And who took the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the video -- this was the voice of the commentator. This is something that we can exclude and you do not need to assess that. I understand that. However, we were unable to cut it out of the clip. All other audio sounds are those by people who were issuing orders, "Kill, torch" and so on. This is a documentary that was made and we are not showing it in its entirety, no. We are showing only the pieces that were filmed in Sarajevo on the 2nd of May, at the time when a lot of soldiers were killed. These were all authentic documentary clips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who made the documentary? You say it's authentic but you haven't satisfied us. Who made it? And how are we to know who is speaking? How are we to identify the persons who are speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the voice of the commentator. However, the orders were issued by voices of unidentified people, and you can hear what they are saying, "Kill, destroy, torch," and so on. This is the film that was made by the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior team for investigating and documenting war crimes. This was made by them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When? When?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The documentary was filmed or rather the clip was filmed on that same day, the footage, and there are statements following that given by various personalities at the time, Ganic, Izetbegovic and so on. I selected only the authentic documentary footage that is self explanatory. I did not include any of the statements given by these persons. No. This is the film made by Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior team for investigating and documenting war crimes. All of this went through the official channels of state Prosecutor's Office in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I received it from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let us hear the clip and then we'll make an assessment of it. Please continue. This is for the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It seems that there is one -- another one under the tram and another one on the corner near the trade union centre, behind a pillar. There is one behind the first tram next to the trade union building. OSA seeks urgently more men with OSA and zolja rocket launchers. We are in a bad situation -- they are in a bad situation. They seek help. Fire at them. Destroy them. They are the army are blocked in the streets of Valter Peric from the Zagreb hotel towards Skenderija, towards the constitutional court, and they are trapped there. They need to be destroyed. UNPROFOR is moving to Zagreb hotel. UNPROFOR is on its way to the Zagreb hotel. They will get there soon. They need to be destroyed, destroyed before UNPROFOR gets to the Zagreb hotel. They are in that vicinity. Hey, cameras. Let them stand ready to open fire at the command. Dedo, you will be issued an order when to shoot. For the time being, just stand ready. Message from Zagi, order from Zagi for all units, all movable vehicles of the enemy to be destroyed, prepare incendiary devices and torch everything. I repeat. The units most closest to Dobrovoljacka, block everything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the transcript beyond this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I saw General MacKenzie speak and I did not hear any translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was there a translation to what that person was saying? I wasn't able to identify him as Ms. Edgerton was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours that would have been very useful for the Defence but I didn't want to burden you with that. It lasted several seconds. Before we move to the footage showing imprisoned soldiers but it would be very, very good for the Defence to hear that. We were unable to skip over that. What is important is that we see what happened to the soldiers here, in what state they were in but this is the very end of the clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So do you want us -- you want more to be shown, is that so? All right. Yes, let us have the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the film, a document, and you saw how this all ended. You saw how the soldiers looked like. You could see who carried out the attack. You could see the insignia of the paramilitary forces. You could see who did the shooting on that day, on the 2nd of May. That's precisely what happened in Sarajevo on that day. You saw what was torched, who issued orders for it to be torched, to be fired upon, to be destroyed. You can hear the orders. It is impossible now to establish who -- whose voice it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How are we to know who gave these orders? We heard voices. That's a mystery. Are we to take your word for it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honours, you don't have to assess any of the words uttered. The document, the film, is self explanatory. You could see who did the shooting, who shot from sniper guns, who torched and who killed. If you are going to question a document such as this one, a film such as this one, and this is something that has already been in possession of the Prosecutor's Office of Bosnia and Herzegovina, this was used in various trials, and is still being used in various trials against specific people, about 300 of them, in Bosnia and Herzegovina for these acts. These people are being tried right now. This is an official document of Republika Srpska which was turned over to competent prosecutors who are now trying these people. Of course, my time here is limited. I cannot give you all the facts. I know all the indictments. I have the names of the people who have been indicted for these acts, and this is just a documentary evidence of the crimes perpetrated on the 2nd of May. It would have been good to hear the entire -- to see the entire film of 55 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How are we to know who perpetrated these crimes by looking at that film? I need some assistance on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will assist you. Let us just stop the clip at certain points and then you will see where it -- what it says there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, you know very well when it comes to videos, films, images anything is possible. Some things are true, other things can be fabricated, you can edit, you can manipulate various films. When it comes to this Trial Chamber, we have often heard and seen video excerpts and we always ask to see who shot the movie or the video. And sometimes we even had journalist, reporters, who were here to testify to the fact that they were the ones who shot these images. Today you show us a video clip, we see some soldiers with some signs belonging to the ABiH. Very well. We can see that. However, who shot these images? Who and when? We have seen various images but are these edited images? Is it many different years edited together? Or are these -- did these events happen on one occasion, on one day? We don't know. You tell us that this is a document that stems from the Ministry of Interior of the Republika Srpska. I imagine, of course, that the ministry is able to give us the identity of the person or the institution that shot this movie and this is how the Chamber would be able to judge. These images were shot within the events, we see those insignias. I cannot imagine that a soldier from Republika Srpska was there shooting the movie and the ABiH soldiers were consenting to it. I mean, I have to know -- we have to know who shot these images.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course we have a witness here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we really wish to follow your point and to follow your line of thinking. The purpose of showing us this clip was to rebut the facts included in the adjudicated fact number 29 that says that on the 2nd May 1992, a major JNA attack was launched in Sarajevo. And you are saying that it was not the JNA that launched the attack; it was rather the paramilitaries associated with the Bosnian army, if I understand you correctly. Now, the difficulty I have in concluding this assertion from the video is that I can't see who launched the attack. What I saw on the video clip was soldiers in fight, and yes, indeed, they were wearing the insignia of the paramilitaries associated with the Bosnian army. But I can't conclude that this was the ABiH that launched the attack. It could have been but it could just as well have been the JNA who had launched the attack. What I saw were just soldiers in fight. And then I ended up seeing a number of prisoners, which suggests perhaps that that battle was lost by the JNA, but I can't be sure. I simply have a difficulty in accepting what you are trying to prove to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, this event of the 2nd of May was testified about by many people here. That's the date when the Yugoslav People's Army tried to leave one of the barracks and this is what happened. This document is as it is. You can, of course, question its authenticity and I don't know what decision you will take on this but we have already admitted into evidence in this case the firing on the Presidency, the Markale shelling and a number of video clips that were tendered by the Prosecution and this despite some of the objections that we made about how the footage was filmed and so on, but documents were always admitted. The video clips were always admitted. Now we have a self-evident document. You cannot see a single soldier attacking. You can see that only the paramilitaries are firing their weapons from the corners where everything that was around it was torched, where the order was issued to burn, torch, everything. You saw what the troops looked like at the time when they were captured. But the footage shows quite clearly how the people in Sarajevo, those paramilitaries, operated. If you look at the insignia on the persons using the sniper rifles, you will see some insignia that used some Turkish words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll admit the video. Of course, the Chamber will have to make its own assessment as to the weight to be attached to what is shown in the video. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it has been brought to the Trial Chamber's attention that you did not object to adjudicated facts 1 to 53, and that includes, of course, the adjudicated facts that you just brought to our attention and to which this video relates. I'll just read from the Trial Chamber's decision on adjudicated facts: "In its response, the Defence submits that proposed facts 1 to 53 concern the general context of the conflict with respect to the acts allegedly committed by the accused, response paragraph 8, and defers to the Trial Chamber's decision with regard to those proposed facts, response page 3. While the Defence here states that it takes no position with regard to proposed facts 1 to 54, the Trial Chamber notes the Defence's submission that it does not object to proposed fact 54. The Trial Chamber will interpret the Defence submission as being that it takes no position only with respect to proposed facts 1 to 53." Mr. Tapuskovic, were you aware that you had not objected to facts 1 to 53, which, of course, include proposed facts 29, 30, 31? I think the video, I believe, related specifically to proposed fact 29. In light of that position, how can you then seek to lead evidence to rebut fact 29?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when it comes to paragraph -- or adjudicated fact 29, rather, I cannot challenge the fact that on the 2nd of May 1992, President Izetbegovic was in Lisbon attending negotiations and that a major attack was carried out on the centre of Sarajevo. But what I'm saying is that the paramilitaries carried out this attack. I'm not challenging the claim that a major attack was carried out on Sarajevo but I categorically claim on the basis of the evidence that I obtained, that it is no longer possible to claim that a major attack was carried out without an agent. I categorically claim that on that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The matter is quite simple. You did not object to proposed facts 1 to 53, which includes fact 29 which says that a major JNA attack occurred on the 2nd of May 1992 on the centre of Sarajevo. You did not object to it. So it's not -- you're not entitled now to bring evidence to dispute that. And I take a very dim view of that, because you're an officer of the Court and must act accordingly. In the light of this, all the evidence that has been led in relation to this matter will be disregarded by the Trial Chamber, and the -- we rescind the decision to admit the video. Please move on to the next area of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to say something in this regard. The Defence has been injured, prejudiced, by this decision. In my view, I have the right to call evidence that pertains to everything that the paramilitary units had done. The paramilitary units are the cause, at the heart of all the developments in the Sarajevo theatre where the conflicts occurred and there is a whole series of things. I mentioned only this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not hearing you because I don't consider your conduct to have been appropriate for an officer of the Court. You did not object to proposed fact 29. It's as simple as that. And so it's not open to you at this stage to lead evidence to rebut it. You should have considered your position before deciding not to object to proposed fact 29. And I don't wish to hear you on the matter. Let's move on to the next area of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to tell you even if I were to suffer consequences of that, I'm not an officer of this Court. I'm the Defence counsel for the accused Dragomir Milosevic. I don't know whether I got the right interpretation of this term but I'm trying to do my job as well as I can. I am not an official of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Every lawyer here is an officer of the Court. It includes the Prosecution and the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first you decided to admit this and then you made your decision, and I have to say something, I have to object to it. This is the first time that something like this was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have heard what you have said. We've heard what you have said. And you should now proceed with the rest of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, what did the paramilitary forces do in this time period before your withdrawal from Sarajevo? Is this the only thing, the thing that you just saw?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the 15th of April, when the Territorial Defence Staff of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued its order, the paramilitary units in Bosnia stopped existing. In this order, they ordered that all those units should be placed under their command. So as of that date, the armed forces of the federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina were more active, as you can see for yourself on the 2nd of May, the JNA as an armed component was not present there. No armed elements of the JNA were there. It was a supply unit, a quartermaster unit, that was bringing dinner and so on to the troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is no translation into French?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Into French, there was no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has that matter been attended to?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, it's fine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just continue. Mr. Tapuskovic, continue. It's not necessary for him to repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So did you see the sniper sights on the rifles and all those insignia? How many paramilitaries were there before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: To what adjudicated fact does this relate now, Mr. Tapuskovic? And I hope it's not one of those that you have already accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not accept the facts -- any facts except the general fact, and even those general facts have their background. These are not facts that are beyond any dispute. A fact cannot be carved in stone. It can be unassailable in some parts but it cannot be ossified. My general attitude is that general context is general context, but general context is not set in stone. I did not take all those facts for granted. Those facts contain many things that have to be elaborated further. I cannot challenge the fact that two plus two make four but I can challenge the facts that pertain to the facts that are not set in stone, that are not beyond dispute, not as a whole. So there are no facts that could not be elaborated further. So it is my view that this attitude that is taken that these facts have been adjudicated and they have been set in stone to such an extent that I cannot dispute them. Yet, I can challenge them because if one fact is true, that Izetbegovic was in Lisbon attending negotiations and then next fact is something that I can challenge, perhaps I -- if that is so, if all those facts are not to be challenged, then I don't have to call any evidence. The adjudicated facts do not have the status of a fact that cannot be addressed by anyone and that cannot be placed in a broader context. That is contrary to any legal logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But Mr. Tapuskovic, the procedure is simple. If you didn't agree with the fact, you should have said so at the time. Because there are other facts that you clearly disputed. There is a whole set of facts that you disputed. But in this particular category from 1 to 53 you accepted them. You did not object to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, Your Honour, we fail to understand each other. Even though those facts may be accurate when it comes to certain information and certain dates, they cannot be considered as something that cannot be contested. These are the facts that can be elaborated upon, completed, that can be further broadened. There are no such absolute facts that cannot be worked upon. This documentary material and this witness, for example, they cannot be excluded because I apparently accepted some adjudicated fact. No fact can be given these qualities, namely that it is unassailable, that it is sacrosanct and frozen forever and ever. I do not wish to dispute the position of the Chamber, but to believe that for those reasons a context cannot be broadened, and that a fact cannot be further elaborated, I have to say that it is contrary to the interests of justice. It is my opinion. Perhaps it's wrong, but it is my opinion. If this film, if this footage, is not sufficient to illustrate the activities of paramilitary formations, which are mentioned in a lot of places throughout the judgement, then I do not understand how come I'm not allowed to broaden some facts, even if I myself consider them to be adjudicated facts. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, you may put questions about 1992, because that's part of the case. The issue arises when you're seeking to rebut a specific adjudicated fact that you have already accepted. And that was the case in relation to adjudicated fact number 29, because you had two approaches, two responses to the adjudicated facts proffered by the Prosecution: Some, you accepted, and this falls in that category; and there is a whole batch that you didn't accept. Now, in relation to those that you didn't accept, you are entitled to rebut them. But in my understanding, where you have already accepted an adjudicated fact, it's not open to you to question it during the trial because the whole purpose of -- or one of the main purposes of this system of adjudicated facts in the Tribunal is expeditiousness. Mark you, not at the expense of fairness but expeditiousness is one of the purposes of the adjudicated facts concept, and if a party who has already accepted an adjudicated fact is allowed to reopen that fact during court, then that purpose is defeated. But you can, you can, without relying on an adjudicated fact, adduce evidence relating to 1992, because it need not necessarily relate to an adjudicated fact. And as I said before, the issue only arises when you're seeking to rebut an adjudicated fact which you have already accepted. That, I will not allow to you do. But you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I give additional explanation in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. Just proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being put in an impossible situation, Your Honours. I simply cannot proceed with my work if I wish to do it bona fide as it needs to be done, zealously. You know very well when the problem of adjudicated facts was resolved just recently. I have worked previously for two years on this case without adjudicated facts being a factor that needed to be taken into consideration. This was put on the agenda practically a day before the trial began and it was a contentious issue until recently. I believed that there was no need to deal with August of -- with the period before August 1994, with general background information, allegations and so on because that did not seem relevant in view of the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, proceed with the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can I continue with the evidence of this witness who came to testify about 1992? In that case it is completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I have said that you may lead evidence about 1992. You have led evidence in this case about 1992. The Prosecution has led evidence in this case about 1992. What you may not do is seek to rebut a specific adjudicated fact which you have already accepted. Isn't that simple? I don't see anything mysterious about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm afraid of what I might say, so it's better if I just keep quiet. When the time comes for closing arguments, I will say everything that I believe needs to be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, what happened with the JNA in those days? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the footage that I saw, from the 2nd and 3rd of May, I can say that I'm an eyewitness to all of those events. Perhaps it will be clearer for the Court if I say the following because the footage doesn't depict everything. On the 2nd of May, the Yugoslav People's Army did not carry out any sort of an attack, either on Sarajevo or on any other territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 2nd of May, Ejup Ganic, who was representing Izetbegovic who was away, issued an order to block all barracks in the city of Sarajevo, to block the military hospital, command of the 2nd Military District, and to display radically hostile attitude in future towards the members of the JNA. His order was carried out by subordinate units in such a way that they blocked the quartermaster's unit, who was supplying food to the 2nd Military District. They set an ambush for that unit, they opened fire, they destroyed military vehicles, and killed and wounded a number of soldiers. Immediately, or rather at the same time, simultaneously, an attack was carried out against the Yugoslav People's Army's centre where there were just five people, together with the Lieutenant-Colonel. Five soldiers and their Lieutenant-Colonel started putting up resistance until the Lieutenant-Colonel was wounded his name was Bozinovski and it was at that point they ceased with the resistance so that they could get treatment for their superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. In order to stop with this topic, because it's not relevant, could you please tell us this: What was your only goal under those circumstances given what was happening to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The main and the sole goal was to provide medical assistance to the wounded, to evacuate them and to evacuate those who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you. I'm putting questions to you so that we can conclude with your evidence as soon as possible. What was your plan? What was your main plan in relation to the entire army?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It is well known that there was an order in place to relocate the army. The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina had issued an order to relocate the JNA into Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The General Staff, on the 4th of May, issued such an order; namely, that all members of the JNA were to be sent to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that members of the JNA who were from other republics should go to their respective republics. The time for implementation of that order was 15 days. That was the time period during which that order was to be implemented. However, the units of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina blocked the barracks and they did not allow the units of the JNA to leave the barracks in order to get moving towards the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. As a result of that, a group of senior officers headed by General Nedjo Boskovic and Colonel Cadzo started negotiating with the Bosnian government. On the 10th of May, the military hospital was unblocked --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, just a minute, please. We are running out of time. Maybe we will revert to this topic a bit later. You told us what you learned from the reports that you received about what was going on in Slovenia and Croatia. I would like for us to see a document in order to establish whether what you have told us earlier was correct. Let me show you this document, DD01586. Let us see the first page. Please look at the first page.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked. And based on this I can see that the orders and information we received from our superior command were based on this, on the documents emanating from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read the heading, the title, and could you please at least read who was present?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It is quite clear to me, without even reading it, that everybody was present, Drnovsek was present, Mesic chaired the Presidency meeting --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I hope that you were taught how to proceed. Please read what it says here. Please read the title, the date and everything else that is written here. I can't do that on your behalf. Please read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: "Shorthand notes of the 125th session of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia held on the 12th of July 1991, at 10.30. Present: Stjepan Mesic, President of the Presidency."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Please see the page 11 in B/C/S and page 10 in English. Please take a look at the speakers on page 11.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ante Markovic, Veljko Kadijevic. On this page, Veljko Kadijevic, federal secretary of Defence, led the discussion at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. You said Veljko Kadijevic. Please start reading from this section where it says, "Losses in Slovenia."

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: "Losses in Slovenia, on the part of the army as I've told you 144 dead and -- or rather 44 dead and 184 wounded. Current crisis spots in Yugoslavia are, the Knin Krajina, Slavonia, Baranja, Serin, Banja, Kordun, Lika. Possible new crisis spots, Kosovo, Sandzak, western Macedonia, Herzegovina. Armed formations outside of the armed forces --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please stop. Ms. Edgerton is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Your Honour, it looks by the number of this document it comes from the OTP. I actually have two submissions. I hardly think that this witness is in a position to comment on this document, not having been present at the meeting of the former Presidency at the time. I think the document, because it so far predates the period of the indictment is largely irrelevant. But, in any case, if Mr. Tapuskovic wants to tender it from the table even without through this witness, I have no objection to the authenticity of the document. As I said, I think it comes from the OTP. The only thing I would ask is that the full translation be tendered when it's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, what are you seeking to establish by this evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, this document is available through the electronic database of this Tribunal to everyone. Secondly, this witness said that information came from Slovenia about the victims. This document speaks of 44 dead as a result of the events in Slovenia, with a forecast that the same would take place in other regions which is what happened in February, March and other months preceding the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army. This document also speaks about paramilitaries, armed formations outside of the armed forces. This is precisely what this witness was about to speak of; namely, the figures about the numbers of paramilitaries. This is the information that he received through the General Staff at the helm of which was General Veljko Kadijevic. And if you allow him to continue, you will see what happened afterwards and how the paramilitaries transformed into an illegal armed force. The witness will tell you that the information he received through the chain of command was accurate and it's further supported by the content of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is 1992, isn't it? What year is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The document dates from 12 July 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, 1991. So how does this affect the question of the criminal liability of the accused? How does it affect the -- any of the charges in the indictment? Why should we be spending time on this? That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- if any general context is important here, the one that led to the tragedy in this country. Why are facts 1 through 53 important at all? What is the relevance of the general context? Let us not -- I'm telling you, Your Honours, the best thing would have been if we had just dealt with the events from the 8th of August onwards and with the crimes that General Milosevic was charged with. In this manner, any attempt to shed any light on to the tragedy that unfolded in this country is doomed. It is impossible to do it. To the causes of all that. If we are to deal only with the crimes that are the -- that General Milosevic is charged with that would be the easiest thing for the Defence because most of them have not been proven, regarding the murders and so on. And I would be so happy if I found myself in a situation in which I were to defend him just against the charges of the campaign --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton, you have heard the reply. He says the Prosecution by pleading the adjudicated facts prior to 1994, has allowed him to deal with contextual matters and other matters prior to 1994. He says that you have let in this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, at the heart of my submission was that I didn't find it appropriate for this witness, who wasn't at this meeting of the Presidency, to be able to comment on any aspect of the content of the document. And I'm quite happy if Mr. Tapuskovic simply chooses to tender the document from the bar table himself. I have no objection to its admission and its authenticity. I simply rose because I didn't see the point on dwelling on it in great detail through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're not questioning its relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. I said I think it's largely irrelevant because in my submission it has absolutely no bearing on the outbreak of the conflict in Sarajevo in April 1992 and thereafter. It's a contextual document and in my view little more than that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we admit the document. Move on to another subject area. INTERPRETER: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please give the document a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit D341, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what was the attitude of the JNA top, primarily of the General Staff, about what the army should do while it was still in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the view of the superior command, and of the General Staff, was that all the problems and all the issues should be resolved peacefully, exclusively by peaceful means. And that care should be taken to protect the lives of the people, of soldiers, officers, citizens, their families and that as much patience is exhibited as possible and that a team would come from the General Staff to conduct negotiations with the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina about de-blocking of the barracks and the pullout to the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the Yugoslav People's Army, did it have any strategic goal involving any of those locations except for what you said, to save the lives of its troops?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no other goal because if it had any other goals it would not have remained in the barracks. It would have been manning the positions from which it would be possible to carry out those goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to the weapons?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honours. But perhaps we could just establish a little bit more foundation that would go to show the basis of some of this witness's comments about the strategic goals of the entire JNA and the views of the superior command and the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, lay a foundation for this witness's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As the deputy commander for logistics, you told us something about the lives of the troops. At that time, when all these events started to happen, did you have any other goal apart from bringing the soldiers, the young people, out of these areas alive?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: That was the only goal. There was no other goal. And it is very well known to the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what order was issued by Hasanefendic on the 27th of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I know that. I held it in my hands. I read it. He issued an order. I will just relay to you one part of it. That was to block all the barracks, all the military units, that they should be disarmed, captured, arrested, and that as few of them should be allowed to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me now just read to you or I would like you to look at a document just very quickly because my time is running out. It's DD04321. That's page 4 in the B/C/S. And page 4 in the English. But could you please explain to us who was Blagoje Adzic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Adzic, just let me look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
