utterances.text: DD004321. Could you just read the first page? What is it, then?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't see it very well. It says, "Shorthand Notes."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean this part where it says that you have to know that all the communications --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, just to note that as of 1.30 yesterday this document wasn't available in e-court. I'm not objecting to the document but making the observation this is the first time I've been able to see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, why is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in e-court on Friday. It was submitted to the official who had gone to Belgrade. So I really can't understand what my learned colleague is saying, except if her real purpose is to confuse me every time she gets up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I doubt that that is her purpose. But she is not objecting. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagovic, were you not told that when you were shown a document that you have to read what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you whether this is the document, 02942723/GS, here on page 4 in front of me. That's what I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then I didn't get the document that you're talking about because these are the conclusions of the people from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the document 02942 -- no. No. It's a mistake. Just a moment. So in front of me I have a document 02942723. That's document DD004321, the first page discusses the work of the Presidency. That's the shorthand notes of the meeting held on the 2nd of March --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Presidency, the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Ms. Edgerton. And not to confuse Mr. Tapuskovic, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Far from it, Your Honours. That would never be my objective. This document that my friend is referring to now we received this morning, and the Prosecution was not given a translation of the document. I wonder if there is a translation available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a translation available, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already told you, page in English is page 4. I gave you the reference. English page 4. But I wanted us to look at page 1 first. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So do you have in front of you 02942723?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's page 2.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's page 2 on the cover page there is the number that you referenced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read this, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: 23, it says the following, "SFRY Presidency, strictly confidential shorthand notes of the meeting of the SFRY Presidency with the representatives of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: "Held on the 2nd of March 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us turn to page 4 in B/C/S and that's page 4 too in the English version. But could you first explain to me who Blagoje Adzic was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Blagoje Adzic was the chief of the General Staff. And after Kadijevic left the Presidency, he was the acting federal secretary of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, what did he say at this meeting and does this correspond to what you just said just a moment ago regarding this problem that is discussed here and that you were familiar with? Could you please read this?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, okay. I will. "You have to know that all the communications with Krajina --"

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at page 4, this is what I have. The number is 27 of the marking, it's 2942727.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I have 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm not rising to be obstructionist at all, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 3 if that's what you want me to read.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If my friend wishes to tender the document, I have no objection. He's having difficulty with the pages and we are all having difficulty with the electronic system. Again, I have no objection to the authenticity of the document. I'll reserve my comments on relevance and I'm quite happy if he simply tenders the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, don't reserve your comments on relevance. Let's hear your submissions on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As a contextual document, background to the transformation of the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it may have some relevance. And nothing more than that. I was just actually, Your Honour, rising to try and be helpful with respect to the electronic system and the pages to try and see if that assisted Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit D342, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you repeat the date, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the date of the document? This is for the Court deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 2nd of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 2nd?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2nd of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But since this document has already been admitted as a Defence Exhibit, am I correct? Well, since the witness has already given us his evidence and since he read this and since he said what he said, I would like to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It says here that Adzic presented the following view: "As for the fate of the army, it will depend on your fate and what you yourselves do there. All those who think that they can solve all the problems with the army is mistaken. If you don't find a political solution, then you have general chaos and civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So was this your view that you talked about, you, as the army leadership in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This was expressed in the orders that were received to the superior units -- to the subordinate units, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened to the barracks that you left behind and what remained in the barracks and in the depots?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in accordance with the approval of the BH government, the barracks were -- started being abandoned on the 10th of May, starting with the military hospital, and all the equipment and the vehicles, ambulances and so on, were to remain there. And in accordance with an agreement mediated by President Mitterrand, they were supposed to be used by the civilians for civilian use. As for some other barracks, all the weapons that were there, howitzers, artillery and so on, were to remain there and of course, the equipment, certain quantity of combat sets and so on, that all remained. They were the last to leave Sarajevo. That was on the 5th of May. So from the 4th of May until the 5th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Yes, yes. Just a minute. Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. There's no foundation to this answer whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, what is the basis of your knowledge as to the information you've just given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was the stand-in for the Commander of the 4th Corps. That was the most senior unit in the command in Sarajevo. And it was through me that the chief of General Staff regulated all the issues pertaining to the pullout of the JNA from Sarajevo and the area around it. So this is why I had all this information and I indeed published a book on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Oh, you have a book on this topic? You have published a book, you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it entitled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "When the vanquished win."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The vanquished. Well, congratulations. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't want to ask you about the book and the wealth of information therein, but I wanted to ask you what happened with the weapons after the JNA pulled out?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the type of weapons. The heavy weapons remained in the barracks, and units carried their light weapons with them, with the exception of the cadets in the Marsal Tito barracks, from the military high school and academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you among -- in fact, who was the last to leave Sarajevo and does it have to do with those cadets, those children?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. There was a problem regarding the departure of the cadets because the leaving behind of heavy weapons in the hands of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the part of Republika Srpska was a problem. And both leaderships had to reach an agreement, so an agreement was not reached until the 3rd of June, and the cadets arrived in Belgrade on the 5th of June. There were no problems. None of them were injured. But they had to leave all the materiel, all the equipment, all the heavy weapons in the barracks. So they just left without anything as students.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened with the depots? Where were they located, the depots and who took the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The smaller depots were spread throughout Sarajevo and the environs. The largest one was in Faletici. Paramilitary forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina tried to get into these warehouses to get the weaponry. And prior to that, they carried out large quantities of weaponry illegally to say so. Then there was a conflict between the forces of the Territorial Defence of the Republika Srpska and the BH federation forces, and the majority of the weaponry ended up in the hands of the army of Republika Srpska. The General Staff wanted to resolve the issue of the two-thirds, which allegedly belonged to the Federation Army, by providing some of the weaponry from the warehouses in [Unintelligible] if I'm not mistaken. The first contingent arrived on the basis of the agreement with the European Community and UNPROFOR, with General MacKenzie and that arrived to the building where UNPROFOR was headquartered, the PTT building in Sarajevo. However, as soon as the first contingent arrived, paramilitary forces attacked these vehicles, looted the weaponry, and that was it. Everybody was trying to advocate a peaceful solution but it was not to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who kept the majority of the heavy weapons at the time when the JNA pulled out of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the larger amount of weaponry remained in the hands of the army of Republika Srpska because the members who were Serbs responded to the call-up issued by the JNA, whereas Muslims and Croats did not respond to the call-up into the JNA. So that when the JNA pulled out, the Serb members of the JNA remained in Bosnia and the weapons remained in their hands too because nobody disarmed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was more important to the JNA, weapons or young men who were 18 or so?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely the young men who were 18, because had it been for the weapons, the JNA would have resorted to force to unblock the barracks. It would not have resorted to negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tapuskovic. Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, if I could just have a brief moment to speak with Mr. Waespi, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add one more thing? Just to make it clear. When it comes to adjudicated facts, we did not -- we did not contest their veracity. We contested their accuracy. It just occurred to me. My colleague just reminded me. We did not challenge their veracity. We did not bring -- or rather we did not bring into question their relevancy, we brought into question their veracity, their accuracy, and this is what it says in our brief. This is our position. I think that you failed to take this into consideration when ruling on this. Just to make it clear what we challenged was the relevancy of adjudicated facts in our brief or rather, the Defence did not challenge the relevancy of these facts, it challenged their veracity. That's how it was. It all happened so quickly that it did not occur to me to bring up this argument when you ruled on this, but it is clearly stated in our brief that we challenged their veracity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wish I understood what you are saying. I never said you challenged the relevance of the adjudicated facts. I simply said, and I read the passage from the Trial Chamber's decision, that you did not contest adjudicated facts 1 to 53. And the decision said specifically, expressly, that you deferred to the Trial Chamber's decision with regard to those proposed facts. Ms. Edgerton? I don't wish to hear any more on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, are you able to hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions based in part on some of the things you've said today and I'll try and be as brief as possible. And perhaps we could start with some things you may feel that you're in a position to agree with. For example, sir, and is your proper title General or Colonel, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I have the rank of a Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, would you agree with me, since you were in place in Sarajevo during -- between 1991 and 1992, that the JNA 4th Corps was effectively the nucleus of what became the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It only appears to be so for the simple reason that the 4th Corps was manned by conscripts from Sarajevo and the vicinity. When the JNA mobilised young men, it was only the Serbs that responded. The Muslims and the Croats did not respond to the call-up into JNA. So that the units were manned by the Serbs from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, about 90 per cent of them were. When the JNA pulled out and moved into the territory of the SFRY, it was only the Serbs who remained, and they became free. Just as the Muslims and the Croats could go and join their own forces, so could the Serbs. So that practically speaking, all of the units established in the territories of the former Yugoslav republics had their nucleus in the members, former members, of the JNA and Territorial Defence, which were -- which had been two components of the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So in essence you would agree with me, then?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree to the extent that this was just a renamed corps. No. It wasn't just renamed. They established a new command, a new organisational and establishment structure, new units, but there were members of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps who had been previously members of the 4th JNA Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And were those largely the commanding officers, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Few senior officers moved from the 4th Corps to the Romanija-Sarajevo Corps. More came from other republics, more of them came from other republics, including Territorial Defence and Serbian generals, one of them being General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to ask you to turn, in one of the binders my colleague, Mr. Registrar, has, to a document that bears the number 03460. The tab is about halfway through your binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I think copies have been made available to Your Honours. One copy has been made available to Your Honours. It is in e-court however, 03460. I'm told by my colleague, Ms. Bosnjakovic, that everybody has a binder available.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document bears my signature. However, I never wrote such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wasn't sure based on the video screen I see in front of you that you were actually able to see the document, sir. Have you got in front of you a document with the heading, "4th Corps command" dated 17 May 1992, which says: "On the basis of the command of the 2nd Military District order dated 14 May, in aim to change titles of units of the 4th Corps in time, we submit to you new titles of former units of the 4th Corps." And as you said it bears your signature on the bottom, sir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It is my signature. This is my signature. However, I never wrote this. Never. Because it says -- it has initials NG -- MG, as though I typed this order myself. There is a stamp and my signature but I can assure you that I never wrote such a document, because prior to this, I tried to --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel. Please, just a moment. We have a question from a member of the Bench here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to see whether I have [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's also published in e-court, Your Honours but you're more than welcome to have my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you said this document bears your initial on the bottom but it's not a document that you wrote. Does that mean it's a document written by one of your subordinate officers?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that. I personally did not sign such a document ever. However, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, I don't quite understand. If you didn't sign the document but your signature appears, are you disputing the authenticity of the document? Or is the document consistent with what was going on on the 17th of May, in terms of the restructuring of the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I am familiar with the names of these units, these units were in existence after the 20th of May, after the corps had been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you disputing the accuracy of the document --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: And I did not participate in the establishment of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you disputing the accuracy of the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a forgery. This is not an accurate document, as far as I'm concerned. It's possible that the names of the units coincided. However, I was not competent to issue such an order.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On what basis are you claiming that the document is a forgery, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Because the -- this shows that the establishment of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was analogous to the establishment of the 4th Corps, and the 4th Corps disbanded practically on the 20th of May. I was there, the only one who remained. I also had an assistant for political affairs. We had two aides and a driver, and that's all who remained there. The other command and the other commanders established the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps using most likely members who had previously been members of the 4th Corps. And I would have remembered if I had --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You would have remembered if you had what, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: If I had written such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But is that not your signature on the bottom, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It is, but it's not difficult to analyse somebody's signature and to put it on another document. They had a stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you saying that your signature has been forged on this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it was forged. Nobody could forge it to this extent. It is my signature. But the content, everything above the signature, is something that I do not remember or that is to say, I was not competent to rule on these issues, to issue such an order. Because there was a different officer who was in command of the corps and it was within his competency to establish a corps with such an organisational and establishment structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, sir, you've already testified that you had been appointed to act on behalf of or in, if I could find your exact words, you were appointed representative of the corps commander of the time. And sir, I put it to you that the -- your successor, the next corps commander, didn't arrive on scene until two days after this document. So that, sir, would put you in exactly the position in which you could issue a directive renaming elements of the 4th Corps and giving them titles that they would carry on as elements of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Had I done this, I would have needed to receive an order from my superior command, which at that time was the 1st military district, in order for me to do it in this way. However, my order was that all members of the 4th Corps who were citizens of the SFRY, soldiers, officers and civilians serving in the army, were transferred to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; whereas members who were from Macedonia, Croatia and other republics could go to their respective republics and join formations there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, you've said you didn't have the capacity to issue such an order, but I'm putting to you that's exactly the capacity that you've testified that you held at that time. You were representative of the corps commander pending the arrival of your successor, and your successor hadn't come on to the scene yet.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody succeeded me in the 4th Corps. I was in command of the 4th Corps of the JNA, whereas Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was established independently of the 4th Corps. But members of the 4th Corps, which was logical, who were from Bosnia-Herzegovina, became members of the SKR. To make it more clear, the government of Republika Srpska offered me to be a commander of that corps and I refused. Similarly, the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina also offered me to become commander of the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I rejected this offer as well. I told them that it was their task and that they were to deal with it and I proposed General Mladic for that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Edgerton or, rather, witness, on the 17th of May 1992, you were in theatre. Do you at least recognise the fact that the titles of units that changed here, those titles that changed and that figure on this paper, on this piece of paper, did this happen or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The names of units of the 4th Corps of the JNA are correct, and I'm not familiar with the names of units within RSK -- SRK. I'm not familiar with the process of organising and establishing the units within Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I'm just not knowledgeable about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you were the commander and you recognise the changes that took place here did take place indeed, but you are telling us that you are not the one who drew or who wrote, rather, this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't within my competency. If you know how the army is structured, you will know that I cannot write to someone as to how to organise and establish a corps without being its commander. Had I been the commander of that corps, then, yes, I maybe would have written this but I wasn't. On the left side, you can see the names of the units of the corps that I commanded as a stand-in commander. But then on the right side you see that it says -- it has other names and those are the units of the SRK that was actually a corps within the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, were you in the habit of signing several documents on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I signed definitely a number of documents, documents that were addressed to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, General Staff, units that were under my command. Yes, I definitely signed many documents. But a document with such contents is just not plausible, could not have received a stamp because it could have been a unit that was part of the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I wanted to ask whether it was perhaps possible that since you signed many orders, many documents, daily, that you might have signed this and forgotten about it. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't hear the answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My signature on such an order would have had no weight, no significance, because in order to establish a corps, that can be done only by the superior command, the command that is superior to such a corps. And the command that was superior to Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was the command of the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska. They were the ones who regulated establishment and organisational issues of their units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, did you sign this document or didn't you, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you maintaining that this document is a forgery, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I told you, Colonel, that this document was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by counsel for the Defence of General Galic, who was at one time commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, would you change your position with respect to the document, with respect to its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. That would not change my position, because legally I wasn't entitled to do what this document does. I wasn't legally empowered to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, my question wasn't about whether or not you were legally empowered, and, with respect, I would suggest that this document only assigns new titles to units. My question was whether or not you would change your position about the document being a forgery knowing it was provided by counsel for the Defence of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I said that regardless of who is the source of this document, I simply wasn't competent to do this because I don't know who would have accepted my order about re-establishing the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We could move on and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: After we've taken the break you may move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I wonder if I could tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies. For the record, I wonder if we could tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First, I object to the -- because the contents of this document have to be compared with paragraph 3 of the indictment. And we should check which brigades were under the control of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and you can see that there is no mention of Pale engineers, the Pale medical and so -- and so two, four, five, six -- eight items have nothing to do with what is stated in paragraph 3 of the indictment. So that's my objection. And also, in light of what the expert or rather Witness said, I wanted to object against the admission but you've already decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I'll reconsider it, absolutely, but Ms. Edgerton, what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it goes to the witness's credibility and I'm entitled to offer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Precisely, it goes to the credibility and so it's -- she's entitled to have it admitted on that basis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as exhibit P912, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, if I could ask you to turn to a further document in your binder, it bears the number 03244. And that document is an order from General Tomislav Sipcic dated 22 May 1995, to the command of the 2nd Romanija Brigade dealing with the organisational and formation alterations in the corps. Have you been able to find that document?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I note that -- well, you said even though you were effectively acting corps commander you didn't have capacity to issue such an order as the formation or consolidation of a military corps. I see by this order, General Sipcic has done that. Now, my question for you is: Is what you read in this document consistent with your recollection of what was going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, would you like my copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is the second time, though. I question the authenticity of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: While we are doing this, Colonel, I wonder if you could deal with my question. Is what you read in this document about the transformation of Bosnian Serb military and Territorial Defence units into elements of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps consistent with your recollection of what was going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I remember when the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was formed, and I know that Colonel Tomas Sipcic was at the head of this command. And probably, or rather not probably but definitely, the command of the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska, which was his superior command, issued him an order to form the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, to establish it. And at any rate, a large part of the members of the armed forces that were in the JNA 4th Corps now made part of this new corps because they were territorially speaking from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: So that this command, the Sarajevo-Romanija command was not in the building where I was at Lukavica. As far as I can remember, it was first in Tvrdinic and then it moved to Pale, to one of the buildings there, a hotel of some sort. I'm not sure what its name was, Planinka or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. So I take from your answer that to the best of your recollection, this document is consistent with what was going on at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that document is already admitted into evidence as to my recollection, P770.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just if I may now, Colonel, a couple of questions about your background. Under the 4th Corps, you said you were the deputy commander of logistics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Assistant to the commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in that capacity, you said you were acquainted with all of the work and all of the activities in the 4th Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And by May of 1992, you were appointed representative of the corps commander after the retirement of General Djurdjevac?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of May, or rather, the 11th, that was when the official order was dated, he was appointed to this post and he was relieved of his duty as the assistant to the commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And by that date, you had actually moved yourself out to Lukavica barracks and that's where you operated from; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I moved on the 1st of April 1992 to the Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was something that you did essentially of your own volition, even though General Kukanjac, the 2nd military district commander, had decided not to move at that time, true?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And from Lukavica, you operated as representative of the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: As the assistant to the corps commander, and then the stand-in. That was as of the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From the 10th of May until what date, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Until I went to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That was on the 5th of June. And on the 6th of June, I submitted my request for retirement, 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, what did it mean, in terms of your function? What did it mean to be stand-in for the corps commander? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I carried out all the duties of the corps commander. That is understood. But I did not have a decree to the appointment -- about my appointment which would have entailed my getting the rank of a general. That's because I refused this kind of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in carrying out all the regular duties of a corps commander, how were you informed of what was going on in the field, in the theatre?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I was in constant contact with the subordinate commands. I was in constant contact with Fikret Abdic, a member of the BH Presidency, with General MacKenzie, with Colm Doyle until the 7th of May, his tour of duty ended then. And I was in constant contact with Colonel Hasan Efendic the commander of the Main Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina and -- and with the leadership of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: By "leadership of Republika Srpska," who in particular are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, specifically we were in communication with the President of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you say you were in constant contact with all subordinate commands, did that mean you were in contact through telephone, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Exclusively by phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Telegram?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: With MacKenzie, with MacKenzie, he'd come to my office regularly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about subordinate levels of command. You said you were in constant contact with your subordinates and I'd like to know how you communicated with them and how they reported up to you.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Using communications equipment, and as for those who were in the immediate vicinity of the Lukavica barracks, we had daily briefings, regular daily briefings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, you were in -- in terms of military control, you were in full, complete control of what was going on in Sarajevo while you were acting as corps commander, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I had full control over members of the 4th Corps, but I did not have full control over the Territorial Defence troops, that was established on the 12th of May by Republika Srpska in an effort to start putting together its own armed forces, its own army.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not only, sir, did you have full control over members of the 4th Corps, but you also had operational control of members of the Bosnian Serb police forces, as well as Bosnian Serb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's already given a direct answer. He did not have any control over the Republika Srpska Territorial Defence troops. So this is repetitive. And only in the end was this last part added about the police force, but the witness said that he had control over the Yugoslav People's Army and had no control over the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I consider that she is putting the question as a whole. So that part which is repetitive can be ignored and the part which is new is to be answered.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, you also had operational control of members of the Bosnian Serb police, as well as Bosnian Serb and Serbian military -- sorry, paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I am objecting to is that the Prosecutor is now putting something to the witness that the witness had already answered. The witness said that he did not have any control. So now the Prosecutor is putting to the witness, so "you had control over the Territorial Defence" and then the question goes on. And he never did confirm that he actually had control over the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the adversarial system, you are allowed to put your case to the witness irrespective of whether the witness -- it reflects the witness's position and this is what I understand Ms. Edgerton is doing. Notwithstanding the evidence that he has given, she is saying, her instructions are that he did have control and so she's entitled to put that to him. Let us hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To finish the question -- to finish the question, Colonel, you also had operational control over members of the Bosnian Serb police and Bosnian Serb and Serbian paramilitary forces who were taking part in actions around Sarajevo at this time, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any powers over the police of the Serbian Republic or of the paramilitary forces or the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic. I cooperated with Stanisic, the Minister of the Interior, if it was necessary to do some work in the area of responsibility of the 4th Corps, just as I was cooperating with minister Delic Mustafic, if anything needed to be done in the area that he controlled.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So as opposed to operational subordination, you're talking about operational coordination, then, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: About the coordination and cooperation. Perhaps this latter term might be a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that also the case with respect to the Serbian paramilitary forces who were active around Sarajevo in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian paramilitary forces and the Territorial Defence in the municipalities had their own commands, and as for the Crisis Staffs we were in telephone contact with them because this was also going on in the area of responsibility of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was this operational coordination -- did this operational coordination with respect to the Serbian paramilitary forces include the Seseljevci who were active in Grbavica and the Arkanovci who had come to take part in operations in Ilidza in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: We did not have any cooperation with Seselj's men or Arkan's men. I don't even remember Seselj's men being present in the Sarajevo area. There may have been in March or April, there was a group at Grbavica in that period. And as for Arkan's men, there were just reports about them in the media, and I am not aware of Arkan or his men being present in Sarajevo while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I then, for everyone's benefit, ask -- and this may test technology a bit, that a telephone intercept be played? The transcript bears the number 03316. The transcript is in e-court. And hopefully copies are in everyone's binders under that tab number. And if everyone has found the transcript, could I ask it be played, please? And I assume Belgrade will advise us if they are not for some reason able to hear it. They also have backup copies there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, did you recognise your voice in the conversation that you just heard?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I recognised my voice and I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also then recognised the voice of your Commander-in-Chief at the time, Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: He was not the Commander-in-Chief, but he was the acting commander of the 2nd military district but he was already -- he was already the chief of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, and the airport was considered to be a -- it was considered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you recognise the voice of Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you hear General Mladic say to Mr. Unkovic from the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Ilidza that the most important thing now is that the military formations, no matter who they belonged to, be put under the command of the 4th Corps headquarters to Gagovic? Did you hear him say that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard him say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you now, having heard Ratko Mladic say that you were to have command of all military formations no matter who they belonged to, do you wish to change your position as to the nature of your command and control over Serbian and Bosnian Serb forces around Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. I can say now that this was an airport, a Yugoslav People's Army was securing the airport. And the units of the Territorial Defence of the Ilidza municipality wanted to take over. And General Mladic here is in a double role, as he is the acting commander of the JNA 2nd Army and the chief of the Territorial Defence Main Staff. In order to prevent the Territorial Defence from taking anything, he is ordering them to place themselves under my command and then I was supposed to deal with all those problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, towards the end of the conversation, did you hear Mr. Unkovic say we have some Arkan's men here and ask General Mladic whether they were under our control? Command, pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that and it cannot be ruled out that there were some Arkan's men at Ilidza because there had been such groups that came in but for such a unit to get there in an organised manner with the connivance of the 4th Corps, that was not possible. I rule that out. But there were individuals and groups of this kind all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Mladic says, "They all are" in reference to the Arkan's men. Now, hearing that, do you wish to change your earlier answer with respect to your operational coordination with the Arkanovci?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot change my evidence because his forces were part of the Territorial Defence of Ilidza municipality with Unkovic and I didn't ask Unkovic about the structure of his detachment or brigade or whatever it was, whether they hailed from Ilidza or whether they were volunteers come from I don't know where.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could I ask that this be tendered as the next Prosecution exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 913, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to move on to another area, you said in your testimony in chief, Colonel, that your prime preoccupation, your overriding preoccupation in May of 1992 was the safety of the young persons in the barracks. You wanted nothing more than to get those young people out. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But actually, sir, that wasn't your only preoccupation at that time. You had another significant task, as we've just heard by your own testimony and in this intercept. You were commanding Bosnian Serb forces that were working towards the division of Sarajevo, weren't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not in command, because the Serb forces that worked on the division of Sarajevo, well, that was not done by the military. That was done by the politicians. Territorial Defence units were set up by Crisis Staffs in the areas where Serbs were in the majority, Lukavica, Rajlovac, Zlatiste, Ilidza and so on. And they -- their only purpose was to protect the homes and lives of the inhabitants living there. There was no intention on their part or on the part of their superior commands or leaders to -- they did not have any designs on Sarajevo. Now, as to what politicians at the higher level did, I didn't want to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But, sir, you've just said you coordinated and consulted with Bosnian Serb leaders and when I asked you who in particular, you identified Radovan Karadzic. Sir, on the 12th of May 1992, the Bosnian Serb leaders promulgated their strategic goals for the coming years and strategic goal number 5 was the division of Sarajevo. Do you not recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that from the press. I remember from the press that they proposed the division of Sarajevo based on ethnic structure. However, no military steps were taken to implement that division.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, if no military steps were taken to implement that division, what would you call the bombardment of the city of Sarajevo on the 14th of May 1992, with such intensity that UNPROFOR and other international organisations were forced to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The bombardment of the city of Sarajevo was non-existent while I was in Lukavica and in command there. There were cases where fire was opened against enemy formations, and when UNPROFOR pulled out, they pulled out because of the fact that one of the mortar units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was opening fire precisely behind the building of engineering when UNPROFOR was headquartered at the Lukavica settlement and other Serbian settlements throughout Sarajevo. This is why we warned UNPROFOR and on the first day they expelled them from those positions and on the second day we were forced to use our artillery to move them out of those positions, because they endangered our lives. There was no bombardment of Sarajevo. Do you know what can be bombarded? Only a city that has no troops. And at the time Sarajevo had 50 to 70.000 soldiers who were constantly opening fire towards positions in Serbian settlements.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, you just asserted that the bombardment of the city of Sarajevo was non-existent while were you in Lukavica and in command there, yet UNPROFOR and other international officials met with Slobodan Milosevic on the 30th of May 1992, to complain to him about the bombardment of Sarajevo. If it was officials of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were responsible for that bombardment, do you think they would have gone to Slobodan Milosevic, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the officials of Bosnia-Herzegovina addressing Slobodan Milosevic, but I know that I was in daily contact with General MacKenzie. Everything that was taking place in the city of Sarajevo was resolved in the triangle between Fikret Abdic, member of the Presidency of BH, General MacKenzie, command of the 4th Corps and command of the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina headed by Hasan Efendic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, I would like -- I'd like us to move on to another intercepted conversation, please. And in your binders, the transcripts appear at 03160. And with Your Honour's permission, there will be this transcript and I think a short videoclip and then I'll be able to conclude with Your Honour's permission. 03160. It's a conversation involving Biljana Plavsic on the 14th of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you testified just a couple of minutes ago that the bombardment of Sarajevo was non-existent at the time that you were in Lukavica. I put it to you that 14 May 1992 was exactly the time you were in Lukavica and the bombardment was such that Biljana Plavsic was complaining about it. Hearing that, do you wish to change your answer with respect to the bombardment of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. That will not affect my answer. This is the reason for that: From the building where the mother of Biljana Plavsic was, and Biljana Plavsic went to visit her mother, on that building there were units of machine-guns and snipers, active members of the army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina shooting at the brigade positions in Lukavica. Biljana Plavsic called me about this and I'm surprised that you're not offering that intercept. So it no longer was a civilian building. It became a military objective. And you are not blaming -- you cannot blame the unit opening fire on that building. You should blame the unit that had originally turned that civilian facility into a military one. That's the position of international law. I mean, it doesn't require any deep thinking. That's how it is. They even turned medical facilities into military ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's not the answer to my question, actually, Colonel, but perhaps we can move on. In your capacity as assistant commander for logistics of the 4th Corps, in which you said -- and I repeat -- you were acquainted with all of the work and all activities of the 4th Corps, and as acting commander of what was to become the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in General Djurdjevac's absence, you must have had detailed knowledge of --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: That's according to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- the level of weapons in the possession of your forces, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you must have been aware of the presence of dozens, if not more, of mortar and artillery pieces ringing the city of Sarajevo and aimed at the city centre all under the control of your forces. Weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's not exactly how it was. There were units and weapons of the 4th Corps. However, there were also units in the city of Sarajevo itself, in possession of both artillery pieces, mortars, snipers --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about any weaponry in the city. I asked about mortar and artillery pieces ringing the city of Sarajevo and aimed at the city centre. In fact, sir, they were there, they were seen there from as early as October of 1991. Are you asserting you weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: In October of 1991, I don't think that there was anything there because in December of 1991, in the corps command, Alija Izetbegovic came to visit. He came to visit us in mid-December, and he informed us about the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Simultaneously telling us that they would organise a referendum for an independent state of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Colonel, are you asserting that you weren't aware that they were there by October 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: They were where? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if all of these facts are undisputed facts, then I am wondering why are they being put to the witness? If I was not allowed to dispute established or adjudicated facts, then I don't see why is it necessary for the Prosecutor to put any questions relating to adjudicated facts. If all of this has been established as is the position of the Prosecution, then why is the Prosecutor allowed to put any questions relating to the adjudicated facts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does this relate to an adjudicated fact?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It relates to his credibility, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Credibility, yes. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's very easy to say so, that it has to do with the credibility, whereas in fact it pertains to the substance of the problem. However, you have allowed this question, so there is nothing I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sir, to go back to the question, when did you, who you say -- you said you were acquainted with all of the work and all of the activities of the 4th Corps and were you acting commander of the predecessor to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, when did you become aware of the presence of heavy weapons and artillery and mortars in the hills ringing the city of Sarajevo aimed at the city?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The presence of artillery weapons around Sarajevo was a fact but only once the JNA units pulled out of Kiseljak and Visoko. In Lukavica there had already been two units of the JNA. As for the Territorial Defence at the time we had no contact with them and we knew nothing about their activities. You are mentioning mortars, and those were most likely weapons that had been confiscated by police at the chicken farm, and somebody wanted to smuggle that from Pale to Ilidza. Other than that, in October of 1991, there was even no hinting that there would be a conflict in the territory of Sarajevo and Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were simply preventing paramilitaries from getting armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When, then, were the weapons placed there?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was sometime -- I don't know the exact dates, but sometime in April, those units relocated from Kiseljak and Visoko to Pale and Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you asserting --

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Those were the units of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you asserting, sir, that the hundreds of mortar and artillery pieces ringing the city of Sarajevo and pointing at the city centre were only brought there in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Which units brought them there? As the assistant commander for logistics, you would know, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know. The units of the 4th Corps. The 4th artillery regiment and the 4th anti-armour regiment of the 4th Corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the 216th Mountain Brigade as well, sir, isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: The 216th Mountain Brigade was headquartered in Han Pijesak, and it was brought to Lukavica only once they started blocking the barracks and it was under the command of General Milosevic, who was under siege at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question, sir. The 216th Mountain Brigade was one of the 4th Corps units responsible for the placement of heavy weapons in positions around Sarajevo, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. The Mountain Brigade, as its name indicates, has no heavy weaponry. Its largest calibre weapon is a 120-millimetre mortar. In the newly-established category, it is known as infantry weapons because those are weapons that are carried by horses and so on. And that unit did not arrive in the territory of Sarajevo until the conflict had begun, which was sometime in May or later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just tender that Plavsic intercept, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as Exhibit P914, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend, you said that you and your command post moved to Lukavica at your own initiative. Why did do you that?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I did that on the 1st of April 1992 because it was my assessment that it was impossible to ensure supplies and carry out my orders in the location where I was, which was in Bistrica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there something else going on that prompted you?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally, there were things going on, march events involving paramilitary formations in Sarajevo and the vicinity indicated that there was a risk that the units in the barracks in Bistrik would be blocked and that we would be basically in the hands of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what about Lukavica in geographic terms? Can you describe its position in relation to other geographic features?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: It is in the northwestern part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a suburb of Sarajevo in a way.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we are getting into the geography around Lukavica barracks, I would submit that's not something that arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does it, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It certainly arises. My learned friend kept saying that the JNA was on the hills, and I wanted to put it into perspective. I wanted us to see where Lukavica is and I wanted to establish whether the JNA was at Hum, Zuc and other positions. Because my learned friend mentioned the hills saying that the JNA had its positions in the hills and I wanted to establish where Lukavica was, whether it was a hill and what was located at Zuc, Hum and so on. Whether artillery units of the JNA were positioned there or not. I wanted the colonel to tell us that if he still remembers it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're point, Ms. Edgerton, is that your cross-examination was confined to specific geographical areas?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question to my cross-examination strictly related to at what time he became aware -- my cross-examination question specifically related to at what time the witness became aware of the placement of mortars and heavier weapons in the hills around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, put the question directly as to whether Lukavica was on the hills or on the plains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please answer the question that the Chamber insists upon? Was Lukavica on a hill? Would you just explain its geographic position?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: No. It wasn't. Lukavica has -- is 530 metres above sea level, just as Marindvor is. So those are not hills. And secondly, one does not position artillery weapons on a hill. I am not here to educate anyone. I'm just telling you that the units of the 4th Corps were not positioned on hills. The 49th Mechanised Brigade was in Lukavica with its forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. You spoke about the formation of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Can you tell us what weapons, what troops, and what officers were placed under the command of the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: I said something earlier and now let me tell you something more about what Alija Izetbegovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Stop. Same point?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Way outside this time, I would suggest, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This doesn't arise. Move on to another question, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I perhaps reformulate? Perhaps if I can reformulate my question, I may have led the witness. I wanted to ask what the 1st Corps of the BH army was established of.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the corps that were established in the area of the former Yugoslavia were founded on the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, either JNA or the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That doesn't arise either. Move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please look at document that speaks to -- well, perhaps the best thing would be to conclude my re-examination and not to ask any more questions. Thank you very much. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILOSAV GAGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, as you had informed us earlier that you don't have any other witnesses, and the Chamber accepted your explanation, we'll adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.37 p.m.,
